clue.text: Cold water poured over one to say "Please be quiet"?

indicators.note: saying something means voicing it, so the request that follows is judged by its sound rather than its spelling

parts.note: a polite plea for silence: 'do' plus the hushing noise 'sh'

explanation.surface: Someone is drenched with cold water as a blunt way of telling them to pipe down.
explanation.walkthrough: DOUCHE is said 'doosh', which matches 'do sh!', an urging to hush.
explanation.definitionFit: A douche is a jet or shower of water directed onto the body, here a cold dousing.

clue.text: Report of high table in deal indicates a cultural ignoramus

indicators.note: placing these pieces in the wood word means it wraps around them

parts.note: deal is softwood timber such as pine; it forms the outside

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the next word is replaced by one that sounds the same

parts.note: the greeting sounds the same as 'high'
to table is to list, and a table is a list of figures

explanation.surface: Talk of the dons' high table in some deal reveals someone who is uncultured.
explanation.walkthrough: Deal is the timber trade's word for softwood. High table is the dons' dining table at an Oxbridge college, which makes the surface sound cultured.
explanation.definitionFit: A philistine is a person hostile or indifferent to art and learning, named after the Biblical enemies of Israel.

clue.text: Building after war — that's why he aided us

parts.note: Mars is the Roman god of war
a hall is a large building

explanation.surface: Reconstruction after a war explains why a particular man came to help us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' places the building word after the war word. The whole clue also points at the Marshall Plan, which funded rebuilding in Europe after the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: George Marshall, US Secretary of State, gave his name to the plan that sent American aid to postwar Europe.

clue.text: Ali's (not his first) heavyweight victim

indicators.note: 'not his first' tells us to drop the opening letter of the boxer's name

parts.note: Ali's without its first letter
a ton is a heavy weight

explanation.surface: A heavyweight boxer beaten by Muhammad Ali, though not the first man Ali beat.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: Sonny Liston lost his world title to Ali (then Cassius Clay) in 1964.
explanation.definitionFit: Sonny Liston was the heavyweight champion whom Ali defeated twice, in 1964 and 1965.

clue.text: Field where the choo-choo is hard to chew

parts.note: a lea is a meadow or field
taken as written
a choo-choo is a train, so a railway, abbreviated RY

explanation.surface: A field where a toy train turns out to be tough on the teeth.
explanation.walkthrough: Choo-choo is a child's word for a train; RY is the standard abbreviation for railway.
explanation.definitionFit: Leathery food is tough and dry, like leather, so it takes a lot of chewing.

clue.text: Gas pipe left off — how much off?

indicators.note: food that is off has gone bad, so the letters are spoiled and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Someone has left the gas off and asks how much has been lost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off' appears twice: first it stirs the letters, then 'how much off?' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Slippage is the amount by which something falls short or drifts from a target, so it measures how far off it is.

clue.text: Explosive bits spoiled her plans

indicators.note: something spoiled is ruined and knocked out of shape, so the words are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An explosion blew her carefully laid plans to pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrapnel is the fragments of a shell or bomb scattered by its explosion.

clue.text: Press (the Queen's) after all points to soft food

indicators.note: 'after' places the royal piece behind everything that comes before it

parts.note: all four compass points: north, east, west, south
pap is soft mushy food for babies or invalids
ER, Elizabeth Regina, plus the possessive S

explanation.surface: The Press, the Queen remarks, are pointing their fingers at baby food.
explanation.walkthrough: ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, the late Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: The press is the collective term for newspapers and the journalists who write them.

clue.text: I get up early for fun

definitions.note: a first-person description of the answer, a noun
definitions.meaning: first meaning: an early riser, like the bird that sings at dawn
second meaning: a bit of mischief or amusement

explanation.surface: Someone says they rise at dawn because they enjoy it.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue speaks as the answer itself: a person who gets up early is a 'lark', after the dawn-singing bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A lark is an early riser, and a lark is also a prank or bit of amusement done for fun.

clue.text: Each dish is eaten by a champion

indicators.note: whatever is eaten goes inside the eater, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: an ace is a champion, an expert performer
a pie is a dish

explanation.surface: Each serving is wolfed down by a champion eater.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Each' at the front looks like part of the picture of servings, but it is the whole definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Apiece means for each one or per item, as in 'a pound apiece'.

clue.text: Trouble at school? Dunce has to crawl about outside

indicators.note: the rearranged letters stand outside, wrapping the other piece
turned about, the letters move round into a different order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
an ass is a fool or dunce

explanation.surface: Trouble in the classroom: the dunce has to crawl round the outside.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is playful: 'school' points at a class, but class war is conflict between social classes.
explanation.definitionFit: Class war is conflict between social classes, cheekily read as fighting in a school class.

clue.text: See 18
Sententious in referring to the past about the pub

indicators.note: 'about' means going round, so the tense word surrounds the drinking place

parts.note: the aorist is a Greek past tense
PH, public house, is the map abbreviation for a pub

explanation.surface: Someone pompously moralising while reminiscing about the old local.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Referring to the past' tempts HISTORIC, but the word needed is the grammar term from the Greek aorist tense, with the pub inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Sententious speech is full of pithy maxims; aphoristic means given to aphorisms, short wise sayings.

clue.text: Beast about to catch girl — not fair!

indicators.note: going about something means encircling it, so the animal word surrounds the next piece

parts.note: a brute is a beast
to net is to catch

explanation.surface: A beast is about to seize a girl, and she cries that it is unfair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not fair!' sounds like a protest, but it means not fair-haired.
explanation.definitionFit: A brunette is a woman with dark brown hair, the opposite of a fair-haired blonde.

clue.text: Work of Johnson the painter's at auctions that are coming up

parts.note: RA, Royal Academician, a painter, plus the possessive S

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming up means reading from the bottom upward, so backwards

parts.note: auctions are sales

explanation.surface: A painter's work by Johnson appears at auctions soon to take place.
explanation.walkthrough: RA is a Royal Academician, the usual crossword painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Rasselas is Samuel Johnson's philosophical tale of an Abyssinian prince, published in 1759.

clue.text: Consent to dismantle High Tor?

indicators.note: to dismantle is to take apart, so the letters are pulled to pieces and rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to agree to demolishing a hilltop called High Tor.
explanation.walkthrough: A tor is a rocky hill, especially on Dartmoor; High Tor is a real one in Derbyshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Right-oh is an informal British exclamation of agreement, the same as saying OK.

clue.text: Local authority has a pull with everyone on National Health initially

indicators.note: 'on' here means added onto, so the word for everyone is attached after the health initials

parts.note: a tow is a pull

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letters of the words just before it

parts.note: the first letters of the two words
all means everyone

explanation.surface: The local council has influence and everyone signed up to the National Health Service.
explanation.walkthrough: The National Health is the British state health service, the NHS.
explanation.definitionFit: The town hall houses the local council, so it stands by metonymy for the local authority itself.

clue.text: Badly ventilated returning from scene in Twelfth Night

parts.note: ill means badly

indicators.note: returning means coming back the way it went, so the word just before is read backwards

parts.note: an airy room is well ventilated

explanation.surface: A stuffy room returned from the set of a Shakespeare play.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the second word is turned round; 'badly' stays as it is.
explanation.definitionFit: Illyria is the coastal land where Shakespeare sets Twelfth Night, after Viola is shipwrecked there.

clue.text: Not an utter disaster, but it made an awfully hot saga in the 7 25

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the consoling proverb that things could be far worse

definitions.text: it made an awfully hot saga in the 7 25
definitions.meaning: second meaning, read literally: disasters at sea make dreadful but sensational stories for the press

explanation.surface: A mishap that was not a catastrophe still became a lurid saga in the press.
explanation.walkthrough: The 7 25 is the linked answer NEWSPAPERS. The proverb is taken literally: shipwrecks and sinkings make the worst things, and the hottest news.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying is offered as comfort after a setback, meaning matters could be much worse than they are.

clue.text: Comment by one in 10 and 14 on man (English) with fruit

parts.note: he is a man
E is the abbreviation for English
a haw is the red berry of the hawthorn

explanation.surface: A remark from someone in two earlier answers about an Englishman carrying fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: The ASS hides in both 10 (CLASS WAR) and 14 (RASSELAS); its comment is its bray.
explanation.definitionFit: Hee-haw imitates the bray of a donkey, the remark an ass would make.

clue.text: Like "Gone with the Wind" for the picture industry?

indicators.note: industry is work going on inside a business, so the letters are taken from within the phrase before it

parts.note: the letters straddle the two words, from the end of the first into the start of the second

explanation.surface: Asking what Margaret Mitchell's novel was like for the Hollywood film business.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue doubles as a cryptic hint: the 1939 film of Gone with the Wind runs nearly four hours, the model of a grand Hollywood production.
explanation.definitionFit: Epic describes a long film or story on a heroic, sweeping scale, exactly what this Civil War saga is.

clue.text: A proper rose?

parts.note: surface reading: a true rose, a genuine member of the rose family
setter's reading: a spring flower whose name splits into a word for strait-laced plus rose, so the answer is the first half of that flower

explanation.walkthrough: Split the flower name primrose and its first half is the answer; the primrose is not a rose at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Prim means stiffly formal and proper in manner, correct in behaviour.

clue.text: It's simple to take in the little prince in a financial transaction

indicators.note: to take something in is to enclose it, so one word goes inside the other

parts.note: pure and simple are synonyms
Chas is the short form of Charles, as in Prince Charles

explanation.surface: It is easy to welcome the small prince into a business deal.
explanation.walkthrough: The little prince is Charles, shortened; at the time of this puzzle he was still Prince of Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: A purchase is an act of buying, which is a financial transaction.

clue.text: Forty days with a forty-nine pulse

parts.note: Lent is the forty days of fasting before Easter
IL is a crossword form of 49 in Roman numerals, 50 less 1

explanation.surface: A puzzling health report: forty days of something with a pulse rate of forty-nine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulse' looks like a heartbeat but means an edible seed. Strictly 49 is XLIX, but setters accept IL.
explanation.definitionFit: Pulses are the edible seeds of legumes, and the lentil is one of the commonest.

clue.text: Grouse nearly arrived on the steppe

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the final letter of the next word is dropped

parts.note: come here means arrived, as in 'has come'
a steppe is a vast grassy plain

explanation.surface: A game bird has almost made it onto the Russian grasslands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grouse' looks like the bird but is the verb to grumble.
explanation.definitionFit: To grouse is to grumble or moan, which is to complain.

clue.text: See 7
